chunks: From him, from Fadalah, from Musa ibn Bakr, from al-Hakam, brother of Abu Aqilah, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I have an opponent who demands many false witnesses from me, and I dislike compensating him [for their testimony], although I do not know if that is permissible for me or not.'
He said: 'Has it not reached you from the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) that he used to say: Do not capture/imprison yourselves and your wealth with false testimony?'

So there is no blame on a man in his religion, nor sin from his Lord, if he repels that [false testimony] from himself, just as if he repels with his testimony the removal of a private part [from its rights] or the shedding of forbidden blood, that would be better for him.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to reject false witnesses in court according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the principle of *kaff* (exemption from blame) when using false testimony strategically to repel a greater harm, such as losing a right or property. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) cites Imam Ali (AS) to establish that such deception is not merely permissible but preferable to the alternative, drawing a parallel to protecting one's chastity or blood from unjust seizure. This highlights the Shia juristic view that the preservation of rights often outweighs the strict adherence to truthfulness in specific adversarial contexts.
